title: Yieldedness
hook: Anabaptists speak of letting go of self-will

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord's Day kept: Sunday set apart, whole. Your line was a day set apart. Did you find your quiet hour, and did it stay quiet? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

A man is running across a frozen pond in the Netherlands, and behind him runs the man sent to catch him. The man is an Anabaptist, and his faith is the charge. He makes it across. Behind him the ice cracks, and his pursuer goes through into the freezing water. The man stops. He turns around, goes back out onto the ice, and pulls the officer out. Then he is taken. His name was Dirk Willems, and his story is told in the Martyrs Mirror, a book of Anabaptist martyr stories. A new week, and new rooms: the Anabaptists and the Quakers. Today's word is German: Gelassenheit.

Gelassenheit is hard to fit into one English word. Yieldedness comes close. Letting go. Letting be. Among the Amish, the Mennonites, the Hutterites and other Anabaptist churches, it names a whole way of standing in the world: giving up self-will, to God and to the community. Its pattern is Jesus in the garden the night before he died. He asks for the cup to pass from him, and then he says, "nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." That's yieldedness. Honest about what you want, and still letting go of it. It shows up in ordinary things. Anabaptists speak of yielding to the church's shared way of life instead of standing out from it. In some communities plain clothes are part of that: not a costume, but a quiet refusal to make the self the point. And it shows up in conflict. Anabaptist churches teach nonresistance, taking Jesus at his word in the Sermon on the Mount: "resist not evil." They hear a call to absorb harm instead of handing it back. Other churches read that verse differently, and teach that defending a neighbor can sometimes be right; Christians have held both views in good faith. Now go back to the pond. Self-will said keep running. Gelassenheit said turn around. That's the surprise in the word. It sounds like weakness, like giving up. On the ice it looked like the hardest kind of strength. Yieldedness isn't losing every argument. It's loosening your grip on having your way, so your hands are free for something else.

Here's the practice: find one place where you're gripping. Let your breath settle. Bring to mind a disagreement you're in right now, large or small: the dishes, a plan, an old argument that keeps coming back. Notice where you want your way. Now rest your hands on your knees, palms up. Ask: what would it cost to let this one go? Not every one. Just this one. If you pray, you can say Jesus's words from the garden: not my will, but thine. If you don't, simply let your hands stay open. The bell holds the time.
Gelassenheit. The German word Anabaptists use for yieldedness: letting go of self-will, to God and to one another.
Your line: let go. Today, in one small disagreement, let the other person's way win, and see what it leaves room for. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Amish, Mennonite, Hutterite and other Anabaptist Christians speak of Gelassenheit, yielding self-will to God and to the community; it shapes their life together and their teaching of nonresistance.
